extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary students, and writers of epic/tragedy (creative-writers studying classical poetics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating epic (epopœia) and related poetic forms — meter, diction, use of the marvelous, narration vs. spectacle, and managing probability and ornament. Focused on classical/Aristotelian principles as illustrated by Homer and Virgil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroick verse should be hexameters
rubrics_metrics.description: For the Heroick Verſe, the moſt Grave and Pompow. — Homer began to uſe only Hexameters, which is the moſt Serious and Pompous of them all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained by meter: hexameter combines spondee and dactyl (two equal times) producing stability (Horace's 'spondæos stables'); hexameter suits the grandeur and majesty of epic. Use hexameters for long epic composition; other verse-types are inappropriate for extended epic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mix verse types in an epic
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be more Ridiculout, to mix them al‑ together as Cheremon har done. — an Epopœia entirely compoſed of Iambick or Tetrameter Verſe would be more tollerable than that where thoſe ſort of Verſes, were mix'd with the Heroick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing lively/short meters (iambic, trochee, tetrameter) with heroic hexameter vitiates the poem and makes heroic passages seem ridiculous; avoid combining incompatible meters within an epic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve iambic/tetrameter for motion/action/dancing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Iæmbick, and Tetrameter Verſes; are proper to give Motion, for the Tetrameter is good for Dancing, and the Iambick for Action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these meters for dramatic/actional or lyric/dancing passages; they are too lively and conversational for the serious, majestic tone required in epic narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic admits strange words and metaphors (ornaments)
rubrics_metrics.description: That Imitation which conſiſts in Narration, uſes them much more than all the others. — Epic admits in a particular manner Metaphors, and foreign Words; and ... employs a much greater Number of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pomp and grandeur of epic arise partly from extensive use of metaphors and unusual diction; epic poets may employ such ornaments more freely than other genres, but with artistic judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer narration with characters acting and speaking; poet should 'say little himself'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poet ought to ſay little himſelf, for in that Js 1j not an Dnitator. — Epic Poem ought to be a true Imitation. Homer uſes in his Poem only fo much of the Narration, as is neceſſary ... and makes thoſe he introduced Act, and ſpeak very much.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the fable dramatick within narration: let characters perform and speak to create action rather than relying on heavy authorial exposition; use brief narration only to preserve form and move plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give manners/personality to all things in fable
rubrics_metrics.description: Every thing in his Poems bas Manners. — Animals, the Elements, Plants, every thing hath Manners in Fable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To maintain the true character of fable, attribute manners, passions, or agency even to inanimate things or animals (as Homer and Virgil do) so they function as persons within the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the marvellous more in epic than in tragedy, but preserve probability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Marvellous, ought to be in Tragedy, but much more in Epopœia, in which it goes even to the Extrava‑ gant. — in Epopœia, the Wonderful ſhould excel the Probable, without deſtroying it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic has wider bounds for the extraordinary because events are related rather than staged; however, do not include things overtly impossible or plainly false — lead the reader by a chain of preparation to accept marvels and avoid destroying verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accommodate fictions to the customs/genius of the audience/time
rubrics_metrics.description: A Poet muſt therefore accommo‑ date his Fictions to the Genius, Cuſtoms and Manners of the People, among whom, and the Time in which he lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust the degree and kind of marvels, allegory, and expression to what will be plausible and acceptable to the poet's contemporary audience and cultural context (e.g., Virgil moderated Homeric liberties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer impossible-but-probable over possible-but-incredible
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poet ought rather to chnfe Impoſsibilities, Provided they have a reſemblance of the Truth, than the Poſſible, which gre(t) Incredible with all their Poſſibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose striking, fantastical incidents that can be rendered probable to the reader (through context, character, or preparation) rather than mundane events that strain belief; maintain poetic plausibility even for the impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nothing in the subject should lack a cause; place unreasonable elements outside the action
rubrics_metrics.description: He ſhould endeavour alſo to admit nothing into his SubjeCt, which has not its Cauſe, and if that be Impoſsible, then that which is unreaſonable muſt be out of the Subject, as in Oedipus, the Ignorance of that Prince concerning the manner of Laius's Death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure incidents have plausible causes; if some absurdity cannot be avoided, arrange the plot so that the unreasonable element occurs outside the central action or is otherwise excused/hid so as not to destroy the audience's sense of probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid staging excessively cruel/incredible actions; narrate them instead
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many things which ſhould not come In View, nor paſs beyond the Tiring-room ; ... Let not Medea ſhow her Cruel Rage, And cut her Childrens Throats upon the Stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For shocking, cruel, or unbelievable events, prefer offstage narration or report rather than spectacle; the audience's sight is less easily deceived than their imagination, so move such incidents into narrative voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead the reader to accept miracles by preparation and chain of events
rubrics_metrics.description: The Wonderful may be puſh'd even beyond Reaſon; ... if the Poet has the Addreſs, to prepare his Reader, and to lead him by a long train of things that depend on Miracle, and prevent him from perceiving, the Cheat which is put upon him; ſuch is the Management of Homer and Virgil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use careful buildup (contextual clues, characters' credulity, progressive marvels) to make extraordinary incidents feel credible and avoid jarring the reader's belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix truth with fiction to make fables agreeable (speciosa miracula)
rubrics_metrics.description: He tells Lies, yet made them ſeem like Truth. — Horace call(s) Specioſa Miracula; Plausible, Agreeable Miracles. Homer joins ſome Truth with his Fictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed elements of observable truth or plausible detail inside fantastical episodes so the fiction attains greater probability and delight; this is a deliberate device to charm readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use paralogisms (plausible false reasoning) to render fables persuasive
rubrics_metrics.description: This is properly a Paralogiſm ... the Method which ſhould be obſerved in making theſe Lies; and that Method conſiſts in making uſe of falſe Rea‑ ſonings, or of Paralogiſms, which Ariſtotle calls ... to prove a thing by the Conſequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit natural human tendencies to infer from familiar signs (e.g., pale = in love) to construct plausible-seeming inferences that support improbable fable-elements; use such reasoning sparingly and artfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hide or adorn weak/absurd passages with dictional ornaments
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus ought we to reſerve all the Ornaments of the Diction for theſe weak Places. — All thoſe Places which are either Abſurd or Weak ... ought to be ſupported by all the Ornaments of the Diction; as Homer, Virgil, Demoſthenes and Cicero have happily practiſed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy elevated language, similes, descriptive richness and rhetorical ornaments precisely where the plot or logic would otherwise be exposed as weak, so the reader's attention is captivated and defects are obscured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not ornament passages that have good sentiment or natural manners
rubrics_metrics.description: Thoſe that have either good Sentiments ar Manners, have no occeſion for them. — A good Sentiment never appears better, than in a ſimple Style: Theſe Places which expreſs the Manners, have no occeſion for them neither.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When language communicates beautiful thought or authentic character, prefer plainness and simplicity; excessive ornamentation will obscure rather than enhance moral or character-revealing passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep frequency of grand impossibilities moderate
rubrics_metrics.description: The firſt ... Great and Incredible ... ought not to be too frequent in a Poem, leaſt they be abuſed. The others ... tho' they are Impoſſible, are humanely ſpeaking Probable ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve overtly divine or fantastical transformations (e.g., speaking horses, metamorphoses) for limited, important moments; rely more on incidents that can be rendered probable by context or by the reported beliefs of credulous characters.
